notes.summary: Analysis of variance (ANOVA), developed by R. A. Fisher, tests whether three or more population means are equal by splitting the total variation in the data into parts. Paper 2 asks about its assumptions, degrees of freedom, sums of squares, mean squares and the F-ratio, for one-way and two-way classification.

concepts.title: What ANOVA does
concepts.body:
• Total variation in the data is split into variation between groups (due to the treatments, an assignable cause) and variation within groups (due to chance, called error).
  • If the group means are really equal, both parts estimate the same error variance, so their ratio F should be near 1. A large F suggests the means differ.
  • H0: μ1 = μ2 = … = μk. H1: at least one mean differs.
  • The test statistic follows the F distribution. With only two groups, one-way ANOVA gives the same result as the two-sample t test (F = t²).

concepts.title: Assumptions
concepts.body:
1. Observations are independent.
  2. Each group comes from a normal population.
  3. All populations have the same variance (homogeneity of variance, homoscedasticity).
  4. The effects are additive: observation = overall mean + treatment effect (+ block effect) + error.

One-way classification goes with the completely randomised design (CRD); two-way classification with the randomised block design (RBD).

concepts.title: One-way classification: sums of squares
concepts.body:
k groups, ni observations in group i, N = Σni in all. Ti = total of group i; G = grand total.

  • Correction factor CF = G²/N.
  • Total SS: SST = Σy² − CF.
  • Between groups: SSB = Σ(Ti²/ni) − CF = Σni(x̄i − x̄)².
  • Within groups (error): SSW = SST − SSB = sum of squared deviations of each value from its own group mean.

Example: A = {1, 2, 3}, B = {3, 4, 5}, C = {5, 6, 7}. G = 36, N = 9, CF = 144. Σy² = 174, so SST = 30. Totals 6, 12, 18 give Σ(T²/n) = 504/3 = 168, so SSB = 24 and SSW = 6.

concepts.title: One-way ANOVA table
concepts.body:
SourcedfSSMean squareF
Between groupsk − 1SSBMSB = SSB/(k − 1)MSB/MSW
Within groups (error)N − kSSWMSW = SSW/(N − k)
TotalN − 1SST

Sums of squares add up and so do degrees of freedom; mean squares do not add up. Compare F with the table value Fα(k − 1, N − k): if larger, reject H0.

For the example above: MSB = 24/2 = 12, MSW = 6/6 = 1, F = 12 with (2, 6) df.

concepts.title: Two-way classification (one observation per cell)
concepts.body:
r rows (blocks) and c columns (treatments), N = rc observations. Ri = row totals, Cj = column totals.

  • SST = Σy² − CF.
  • SS rows = ΣRi²/c − CF. SS columns = ΣCj²/r − CF.
  • SSE = SST − SS rows − SS columns.
SourcedfMean squareF
Rowsr − 1MSR = SSR/(r − 1)MSR/MSE
Columnsc − 1MSC = SSC/(c − 1)MSC/MSE
Error(r − 1)(c − 1)MSE = SSE/((r − 1)(c − 1))
Totalrc − 1

Example: 5 rows and 4 columns give df 4, 3, 12 and 19.

concepts.title: Reading the result
concepts.body:
• F is never negative. F close to 1 means the group differences are no bigger than chance.
  • In ANOVA, F is always MSB/MSW. If F is less than 1, the result cannot be significant and H0 is accepted.
  • Adding the same constant to every observation changes no sum of squares, so F does not change. Multiplying all values by a constant also leaves F unchanged.
  • A significant F only says that some means differ, not which ones.

varieties.name: Ideas and assumptions
varieties.how: ANOVA compares several means using an F-ratio of between-group to within-group variance. Assumptions: independence, normality, equal variances, additivity.

example.q: Which of these is NOT an assumption of analysis of variance: (a) normal populations, (b) equal population variances, (c) independent observations, (d) equal population means?
steps: Normality, equal variances and independence are the assumptions.
Equal means is the null hypothesis being tested, not an assumption.

varieties.name: Degrees of freedom
varieties.how: One-way: between k − 1, within N − k, total N − 1. Check that the first two add to the third.

example.q: Five fertilisers are each tried on 6 plots. Find the degrees of freedom between treatments, within treatments and in total.

varieties.name: Sums of squares
varieties.how: Use TSS = SSB + SSW; with raw data use CF = G²/N, SST = Σy² − CF, SSB = ΣT²/n − CF.

example.q: In a one-way ANOVA, the total sum of squares is 150 and the within-group sum of squares is 90. Find the between-group sum of squares.

varieties.name: Mean squares and the F-ratio
varieties.how: Divide each SS by its own df to get mean squares, then F = MSB/MSW.

example.q: One-way ANOVA: k = 3 groups, N = 15, SSB = 40, SSW = 60. Find F.

varieties.name: One-way ANOVA from raw data
varieties.how: Find the group means and the grand mean. SSB = Σn(group mean − grand mean)², SSW = squared deviations within groups. Then mean squares and F.

example.q: Three groups: A = {1, 2, 3}, B = {3, 4, 5}, C = {5, 6, 7}. Find the F-ratio.

varieties.name: Two-way ANOVA
varieties.how: Rows df r − 1, columns df c − 1, error df (r − 1)(c − 1). Each F = its mean square ÷ MSE.

example.q: A two-way ANOVA has 4 rows and 3 columns (one observation per cell). SS rows = 24, SS columns = 30, SS error = 18. Find the F-ratios for rows and columns.

tips: Sums of squares and degrees of freedom both add up to the total; mean squares do not.
Using CF = G²/N saves time with whole-number data.
Subtracting a constant from every value first makes the arithmetic smaller without changing F.
Two-way error df is (r − 1)(c − 1), the same as for a contingency table.
With two groups, ANOVA F equals the square of the two-sample t.
traps: Within-group df is N − k, not N − 1.
F = MSB/MSW uses mean squares, not the raw sums of squares.
Equal means is the hypothesis being tested, not an assumption.
A significant F does not tell you which pair of means differs.

formulas.name: Two-way df
formulas.expr: rows r − 1, columns c − 1, error (r − 1)(c − 1), total rc − 1

questions.q: In analysis of variance, the test statistic used is:
questions.solution: ANOVA compares the between-group mean square with the within-group mean square; their ratio follows the F-distribution.

questions.q: In a one-way ANOVA with 4 treatments and 20 observations in all, the degrees of freedom for error (within) are:
questions.solution: df within = N − k = 20 − 4 = 16. (df between = 3, df total = 19.)

questions.q: One-way ANOVA: k = 4 groups, N = 24, SSB = 60, SSW = 120. The F-ratio is:
In a one-way ANOVA, total sum of squares = 200 and between-group sum of squares = 80. The within-group sum of squares is:
In a two-way ANOVA with 5 rows and 4 columns (one observation per cell), the error degrees of freedom are:
Three groups: A = {2, 4, 6}, B = {5, 7, 9}, C = {8, 10, 12}. The F-ratio for one-way ANOVA is:
questions.solution:
Group means: 4, 7, 10. Grand mean = 63/9 = 7.
SSB = 3[(4−7)² + (7−7)² + (10−7)²] = 3 × 18 = 54.
SSW: each group has deviations −2, 0, 2 ⇒ 8 per group ⇒ 24.
MSB = 54/2 = 27; MSW = 24/(9 − 3) = 4.
F = 27/4 = 6.75.
